text.p: This is how major world bond markets were trading in late European business on Friday.

GERMANY - Bund futures finished the week on a sour note as a several inflation reports and comments from the vice president of the Bundesbank quashed for the moment any hope of an interest rate cut. The March Bund future on the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) was trading at 101.16, down 0.44 from Thursday's settlement price.

BRITAIN - Gilts slipped, wounded by a poor performance from U.S. Treasuries and worries over GDP data and supply next week. The March long gilt future on LIFFE was trading at 110-19/32, down 23/32 from Thursday's settlement price.

FRANCE - French bond futures drifted lower as German regional inflation reports and comments from a Bundesbank official dampened hopes for rate cuts, although traders said it was a relatively calm decline. The March notional bond future on the MATIF in Paris settled at 130.32 down 0.46 from Thursday's settlement price.

ITALY - Italian debt markets ended nearly 50 basis points down on the day but recovered from the session's lows before dealers packed up for the weekend. The March bond future on LIFFE was trading at 131.54, down 0.46 from Thursday's settlement price.

UNITED STATES - The prices of U.S. Treasury securities were slightly lower following a night of active trading overseas. The March Treasury bond future on the Chicago Board of Trade was trading at 110-01/32, down 26/32 from Thursday's settlement price. The long bond was quoted to yield 6.91 percent.

JAPAN - The key March Japanese government bond futures contract ended sharply higher due to cash bond buying by investors and short-squeezing by dealers. In after hours trading the March future on LIFFE was trading at 126.15, up 0.49 from Thursday's settlement price on the Tokyo Stock Exchange.

EUROBONDS - Primary market issuance eased following a week of solid supply. Two borrowers tapped the Czech crown sector, both at one- year for 1.0 billion -- The Canadian Wheat Board via Wood Commerzbank and Dresdner Bank via Dresdner Kleinwort Benson. A syndicate official said the deals were arbitrage-driven and offered yield-hungry investors attractive coupons. Both deals pay a coupon of 10.75 percent.
Sweden set a 150 billion 10-year structured bond via Credito Italiano and Lehman Brothers. The paper pays a coupon of 11.0 percent for two years, then 19 less two times six-month LIBOR.
